title: Balantidium coli Infection
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Balantidium coli is a ciliated protozoan causing balantidiasis, mainly diarrhoea and dysentery. It is acquired from contaminated water or food, especially in low‑resource settings. Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy; treatment is metronidazole or tetracycline.

sections.p: Balantidium coli is the largest known intestinal protozoan, a single‑cell organism with cilia that moves in a whip‑like fashion. It is the causative agent of balantidiasis, a zoonotic disease transmitted mainly through faecal‑oral routes.
The organism is oval, 50–100 µm, with a single nucleus and a prominent macronucleus. It has a ventral sucker for attachment and a single flagellum for motility.
Transmission is faecal‑oral via contaminated water, food or contact with infected pigs. The cyst stage is resistant to desiccation; trophozoites are the active form in the gut.
Balantidiasis presents with watery or bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, fever and tenesmus. Severe cases can lead to perforation, sepsis or death, especially in immunocompromised patients.
Microscopy of fresh stool is the gold standard. Multiple samples increase yield. In low‑resource settings, a simple wet mount is often all that is available.

In a patient with chronic diarrhoea and a history of pig exposure, consider balantidiasis. Microscopy may be negative early; repeat samples improve sensitivity. Metronidazole is effective but avoid in pregnancy unless no alternative.
Giardia lamblia (giardiasis) – both cysts in stool, but Giardia lacks cilia and is smaller. Entamoeba histolytica – causes dysentery but lacks cilia.
Stool microscopy may be falsely negative if samples are old or if the patient is on antibiotics that kill trophozoites. Cysts are fragile and may not survive transport.
Severe dehydration, persistent fever >48 h, bloody diarrhoea, abdominal tenderness suggesting perforation, or signs of sepsis.
